title: Future forms
tagline: Four ways to talk about tomorrow — and B1 wants you to pick exactly the right one.
exam: Writing Part 1 — an email arranging plans
why: B1 Preliminary tests future forms everywhere: predicting a football score, arranging to meet a friend by email, or reading a cinema programme. Mixing up will and going to, or using will after when, is one of the most common B1 errors — and one of the easiest to fix once you know the four clear jobs each form does.

hook.text: Nadia: “I'm going to buy tickets for the concert — look at this queue, it's going to sell out!” Mateo: “I think I'll come too.” Sofia: “Great, I'm meeting Liam there at seven anyway.”
hook.ask: Four future forms appear in bold. Which is a prediction based on evidence, which is a quick decision, and which is an arrangement already fixed with someone else?

watch_out.wrong: I will go to the concert with Sofia at seven, we arranged it yesterday.
watch_out.right: I'm going to the concert with Sofia at seven — we arranged it yesterday.
watch_out.why: An arrangement already fixed with another person needs the present continuous, not will.

watch_out.wrong: Look at those clouds, it will rain.
watch_out.right: Look at those clouds, it's going to rain.
watch_out.why: A prediction based on evidence you can see now needs going to, not will.

watch_out.wrong: The concert is going to start at eight, according to the programme.
watch_out.right: The concert starts at eight, according to the programme.
watch_out.why: A fixed timetable or programme uses the present simple, not going to.

watch_out.wrong: When the concert will start, we'll find our seats.
watch_out.right: When the concert starts, we'll find our seats.
watch_out.why: After when/as soon as/before/until, use the present simple, never will, even though the meaning is future.

watch_out.wrong: I'm sure she going to like the band.
watch_out.right: I'm sure she'll like the band.
watch_out.why: A prediction that's just an opinion (I'm sure, I think) usually takes will, not going to.

watch_out.wrong: I decide to buy a ticket now.
watch_out.right: I'll buy a ticket now — I've decided!
watch_out.why: An instant decision made at the moment of speaking uses will, not the present simple.

l1.es: Voy a comprar las entradas esta noche.
l1.wrong: I will buy the tickets tonight.
l1.right: I'm going to buy the tickets tonight.
l1.why: Voy a + infinitivo describes a plan already decided — that's going to in English, not will.

l1.wrong: I think it will rain, look at those clouds.
l1.right: Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.
l1.why: Evidence you can see right now (clouds) needs going to, even though creo que often makes learners reach for will.

l1.wrong: When I will arrive, I'll call you.
l1.why: Spanish uses the subjunctive after cuando for the future; English simply uses the present simple, never will.
A fixed arrangement with someone else (quedamos) is the present continuous in English, not will.

remember.trick: Plan + evidence = GOING TO. Fixed with someone = -ING!
remember.tip: Can you see the evidence right now, or did you decide before this moment? That's going to. Already arranged with someone else? That's the present continuous.

items.first: Nadia decided before now to buy the tickets online.

can_do: I can make predictions and instant decisions with will, and plans with going to.
I can use the present continuous for arrangements and the present simple for timetables.
I can use when, as soon as, until and before + present simple to talk about the future.
summary: Will/won't = predictions (opinion), instant decisions and promises.
Going to = plans already decided, and predictions based on evidence you can see now.
Present continuous = arrangements with a fixed time and place, already organised with someone.
Present simple = timetables and fixed programmes, even about the future.
After when, as soon as, until and before, always use the present simple, never will.
